title: 'PoK Is Not Part of Pakistan': Thousands Protest in Rawalakot as Azad Kashmir Unrest Enters Fourth Week
excerpt: At least 53 civilians killed as Pakistan deploys army, bans protest movement, and shuts down internet across the disputed territory — while diaspora communities rally in the UK
body:
As the sun sets over the green valleys of Pakistan-administered Kashmir, a region better known for its breathtaking landscapes than its politics, the streets tell a different story. For over three weeks now, cities and towns across Azad Kashmir have been convulsed by the most significant political upheaval the territory has seen in years — protests that have left dozens dead, hundreds injured, and are now raising uncomfortable questions about Pakistan's grip on the disputed region.

The movement, led by the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JKJAAC), erupted on June 7 after the Supreme Court of Azad Kashmir ruled that 12 seats reserved in the regional legislative assembly for Kashmiri refugees living elsewhere in Pakistan are constitutionally protected and cannot be abolished without a constitutional amendment. For residents of the territory, the ruling was the last straw.

"These seats allow people who have never lived here, who have no stake in our daily lives, to decide our political future," one protest organizer told reporters in Rawalakot, the city that has become the epicentre of the unrest. "We are being governed by outsiders, and now even our courts say we cannot change that."

## A Region on Fire

What began as organised demonstrations quickly escalated into violent confrontations. On June 8, clashes between protesters and security forces in Rawalakot and surrounding areas killed between 11 and 15 people and left more than 70 injured, according to regional authorities and media reports. Pakistani Army personnel and Rangers allegedly opened fire on crowds gathered at Rawalakot's Eidgah Ground, where tens of thousands had assembled.

By official estimates compiled from multiple sources, at least 53 civilians have been killed across Pakistan-administered Kashmir since the unrest began on June 5. Seven deaths were reported in Kotli, one in Mirpur, and the deadliest single incident saw 16 people killed in Rawalakot during a protest rally. Hospitals across the region have struggled to cope with the influx of casualties.

The violence triggered a sweeping crackdown. The regional government proscribed the JKJAAC under anti-terrorism legislation, registered sedition cases against four of its leaders, and announced a bounty of 10 million Pakistani rupees (roughly $36,000) for their arrest. Internet and mobile networks were shut down across much of the territory, and helicopter surveillance was deployed over Rawalakot and Muzaffarabad.



> **""This is a people reclaiming their voice after decades of fear," echoed human rights activist Tasleema Akhter on X."**


In a grim twist, one of the military helicopters used for surveillance crashed over Muzaffarabad on June 10, killing all 22 personnel onboard.

## 'PoK Is Not Part of Pakistan'

The protests have taken on an increasingly dramatic tone. At Rawalakot's Eidgah Ground — the same site where security forces opened fire on demonstrators — thousands of protesters were reported chanting "PoK is not part of Pakistan," a slogan that cuts to the heart of the region's contested identity. Local leader Aman Khan issued a stark warning to Islamabad, saying that if food supplies continue to be blocked, people may start looking towards India for support.


![Azad Kashmir — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/70/Neeulm_Valley_AJK_%28Arang_Kel%29.jpg)


JKJAAC leader Shaukat Nawaz Mir described the crackdown as a "massacre" and vowed that the protest movement would continue despite the ban. "This is a people reclaiming their voice after decades of fear," echoed human rights activist Tasleema Akhter on X.

Pakistan Defence Minister Khawaja Asif urged "complete obedience to state" — a statement that critics said underscored the authoritarian approach to what is fundamentally a democratic demand. Prime Minister Faisal Mumtaz Rathore maintained that dialogue remained possible but insisted that constitutionally protected issues could not be altered without following legal procedures.

## International Condemnation

Amnesty International issued a sharp rebuke, describing the response as a "violent and sweeping crackdown" that included "an internet shutdown, mass arbitrary arrests, and deadly use of force," marking a "dangerous deterioration of human rights in the region." The organisation called the government's designation of the JAAC as a terrorist organisation a "dangerous escalation."

The unrest has also spilled across borders. In Bradford, UK, members of the Kashmiri diaspora staged a protest outside the Pakistani Consulate, accusing authorities of excessive force and demanding accountability for the killings. Similar demonstrations have been reported in other cities with significant Kashmiri diaspora populations.

## The Deeper Grievances

While the immediate trigger is the reserved-seats issue, the protests tap into years of accumulated frustration. Pakistan has long been accused of exploiting Azad Kashmir's abundant natural resources — hydropower, minerals, and forests — while leaving its residents impoverished. Basic infrastructure, education, and healthcare remain neglected. The JKJAAC previously led major protests in 2024 over electricity tariffs and flour prices, and in 2025 over a broader 38-point charter of demands.

The region has also faced allegations of demographic engineering and military occupation — charges that have gained new resonance as protesters openly question their political relationship with Islamabad. With legislative elections scheduled for July 27, the protests represent both a constitutional crisis and a broader reckoning about governance, autonomy, and identity in the disputed territory.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For the estimated 1.5 million Kashmiris in the UK and tens of thousands spread across North America and the Gulf, the protests have struck a deeply personal chord. Many retain family ties to towns like Mirpur, Kotli, and Rawalakot — the very cities where security forces have fired on civilians. Social media has been flooded with videos and appeals, even as internet shutdowns within Azad Kashmir have made direct communication increasingly difficult.

The intensity and duration of this movement — now entering its fourth week with no sign of abating — suggests that it represents something more than a periodic eruption of discontent. As one Muzaffarabad resident told Reuters: "These people are not against Pakistan. They are just asking for their own rights."

Whether Islamabad chooses to listen, or continues to reach for the tools of repression, may well determine the future of its relationship with the seven million people it governs across the Line of Control.
